question: We're playing best of five games to 11. In the third game, when do we switch ends?

answer.reasoning: The question asks when ends are changed during the third game of a best-of-five, 11-point match. The standard Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) answer this directly in Law 8.1.3: in the third game when a side first scores 11 points (except in Handicap Matches). The ITTO 5.6.10 corroborates the on-court procedure (umpire calls 'interval, change ends' after the rally that first takes a side to 11 in a third game). The Alternative Laws best-of-5-games-11 format differs: its 8.1.3 replaces the mid-third-game change with a change at the end of the third game if there is a fourth game, and its 8.1.5 puts the mid-game change in the fifth game at 6 points. Both the standard rule and the alternative are given per the format rule.
answer.answer: Under the standard Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 8.1.3: players change ends "in the third game when a side first scores 11 points, except in Handicap Matches (BWF Statute Section 4.1.3)". So in your best-of-five-to-11 match, you switch ends in the third game at the end of the rally in which either side first reaches 11 points. The Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, describe the same moment: "In a third game... after the rally which first takes a side to 11 points... the Umpire shall call the score followed immediately by 'interval, change ends'" (Clause 5.6.10). Note the Alternative Laws of Badminton 2.0, format best-of-5-games-11, in force 2027-01-04, differ: there is no mid-third-game change; instead players change ends "at the end of the third game, if there is to be a fourth game" (Clause 8.1.3), and the mid-game change occurs "in the fifth game when a side first scores 6 points" (Clause 8.1.5).

question: My opponent shouted 'fault!' while I was playing my shot. What's the ruling?

answer.reasoning: The question asks about an opponent shouting 'fault!' during the user's stroke. Two sources bear directly: Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) clause 13.4.5 makes it a fault if, in play, a player 'deliberately distracts an opponent by any action such as shouting or making gestures', and Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) clause 5.9.1.4 specifies that 'A player calling 'fault', etc. to the opponent when making a stroke or after the opponent has made a stroke, shall be considered a deliberate distraction (Law 13.4.5)'. The consequence of a fault is covered by Law 15.3 (shuttle not in play when 'a fault or a let has occurred') and Law 7.3 (the side wins the rally if the opposing side commits a fault, adding a point). Together these fully answer the question: the shout is a fault by the opponent, so the user's side wins the rally and scores. No missing parts.
answer.answer: The opponent's shout of 'fault!' while you were playing your shot is a fault by the opponent. Under Law 13.4.5 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, it is a fault if, in play, a player 'deliberately distracts an opponent by any action such as shouting or making gestures'. The Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, clause 5.9.1.4, confirm this exact situation: 'A player calling 'fault', etc. to the opponent when making a stroke or after the opponent has made a stroke, shall be considered a deliberate distraction (Law 13.4.5)'. As a result, the shuttle is not in play because 'a fault or a let has occurred' (Law 15.3), and your side wins the rally and adds a point to your score, since 'A side shall win a rally, if the opposing side commits a 'fault'' (Law 7.3).

question: When do we replay a rally? List every situation that counts as a let.

answer.reasoning: The question asks for every situation that counts as a 'let' (a replayed rally). Law 14 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, is the dedicated 'LETS' section. Reading clause 14.2 and its sub-clauses gives the complete list: 14.2.1 (server serves before receiver is ready), 14.2.2 (both server and receiver faulted during service), 14.2.3 with 14.2.3.1 and 14.2.3.2 (shuttle caught on/suspended on top of the net after service is returned, or caught in the net after passing over it), 14.2.4 (shuttle disintegrates with base completely separating), 14.2.5 (umpire's opinion that play is disrupted or a player distracted by a coach), 14.2.6 (line judge unsighted and umpire/IRS unable to decide), and 14.2.7 (any unforeseen or accidental situation). Clause 14.1 says who calls the let, and 14.3 gives the effect (replay: play since last service does not count and the last server serves again). A Para Badminton variant (14.2.3.2.1) exists but is not mentioned because the question is not about para play. Together these sources fully answer the question.
answer.answer: A rally is replayed when a 'let' is called. 'Let' is called by the umpire, or by a player if there is no umpire, to halt play [laws-14.1]. When a 'let' occurs, play since the last service shall not count and the player who served last shall serve again — i.e. the rally is replayed [laws-14.3]. Under Law 14.2 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, it shall be a 'let' if: (1) the server serves before the receiver is ready (Law 9.4) [laws-14.2.1]; (2) during service, the receiver and the server are both faulted [laws-14.2.2]; (3) after the service is returned, the shuttle is caught on the net and remains suspended on its top [laws-14.2.3.1], or, after passing over the net, is caught in the net [laws-14.2.3.2]; (4) during play, the shuttle disintegrates and the base completely separates from the rest of the shuttle [laws-14.2.4]; (5) in the opinion of the umpire, play is disrupted or a player of the opposing side is distracted by a coach [laws-14.2.5]; (6) a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision [laws-14.2.6]; or (7) any unforeseen or accidental situation has occurred [laws-14.2.7].

question: My partner cut his hand mid-game and it's bleeding. How long can we stop, and who can come on court to help?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) how long play can stop for a bleeding injury, and (2) who may come on court to help. The Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, cover both directly: clause 5.14.2 gives the rule for a blood-flowing injury (delay until bleeding stops/wound dressed/Referee advises otherwise), clause 3.6.1.4 says the Referee must resolve it 'well within a few minutes' (no fixed minute limit exists), clause 5.14.1 and 3.6.1.1 say the Umpire times the delay, and clause 3.6.1.2 allows only quick relief (e.g., a bandage) on court. On who enters: clause 3.6.1.1 (Referee and Tournament Doctor go on court immediately when called), 5.14.1 (Referee decides who is required), and 3.6.1.3 (maximum two persons on court to assist/advise, with the same allowed for the opposing side). Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) Law 16.3.1/16.3.3 add that the umpire may suspend play for as long as necessary and the score stands. All parts are answered; no refusal needed.
answer.answer: There is no fixed number of minutes. For a blood-flowing injury, the game should be delayed until the bleeding stops, the wound is suitably dressed, or the Referee advises the Umpire otherwise (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.14.2). More generally, the umpire may suspend play for such a period as the umpire considers necessary (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 16.3.1), and if play is suspended the existing score stands and play resumes from that point (Law 16.3.3). The Referee must resolve the injury situation 'as quickly as possible and well within a few minutes so that play can be resumed or abandoned' (ITTO Clause 3.6.1.4), and the Umpire times the delay caused by the injury (ITTO Clauses 5.14.1 and 3.6.1.1). On court, the Tournament Doctor may apply only a quick relief, such as a bandage on a bleeding injury; no time-consuming treatment is allowed except in the regular intervals (ITTO Clause 3.6.1.2). Whether your partner continues is his decision, made as fast as possible after the Tournament Doctor examines him (ITTO Clause 3.6.1.2). Note that play may not be delayed to regain strength or wind (Law 16.4.1), and the Referee may point to potential disqualification if the injury is being exploited to regain wind (ITTO Clause 3.6.1.4). As for who may come on court: when the Umpire calls, the Referee and the Tournament Doctor shall immediately go on court (ITTO Clause 3.6.1.1); the Referee decides whether the Tournament Doctor or anyone else is required on court (ITTO Clause 5.14.1); and the Referee may allow a maximum of two persons on court to assist and advise the injured player and help with translation, allowing the opposing side the same consideration in fairness (ITTO Clause 3.6.1.3).

question: Water started dripping from the roof onto our court mid-game. What happens to the match and the score?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what happens to a match and its score when water drips onto the court mid-game. The Laws of Badminton cover suspension of play and its effect on the score (Law 16.3.1, 16.3.2, 16.3.3), and the Instructions to Technical Officials cover the umpire's procedure when a court becomes temporarily unplayable, the suspension call, and resumption (ITTO 5.11.2, 5.11.3, 5.11.4, 5.11.5). Together these fully answer the question: play is suspended, the existing score stands, and play resumes from that point. No additional searching is needed.
answer.answer: Water dripping onto the court is a circumstance affecting playing conditions, not within the players' control. The umpire may suspend play for as long as considered necessary (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 16.3.1), and the Referee may also instruct the umpire to suspend play in special circumstances (Law 16.3.2). Under the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, if during a match a court or its immediate surroundings is temporarily not playable, the Umpire shall call the Referee and play is suspended until the court and its surroundings are again suitable for play (ITTO 5.11.3); play may be suspended by the Referee or Umpire if warranted by a circumstance affecting playing conditions (ITTO 5.11.2). When play is suspended, the Umpire calls "Play is suspended" and notes "S" on the scoring device or score-sheet (ITTO 5.11.4). The score is unaffected: if play is suspended, the existing score shall stand and play shall be resumed from that point (Law 16.3.3). When play resumes, the Umpire notes the duration of the suspension, ensures the players are on the correct side of the net and in the correct service courts, then calls "Are you ready?" followed by the score and "Play" (ITTO 5.11.5).

question: My opponent keeps flicking sweat onto the court. What can the umpire do about it?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what the umpire can do when a player flick throws sweat onto the court. The directly on-point source is Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) clause 5.9.1.6, which addresses a player throwing sweat or otherwise contaminating the court and says Law 16.7 is applied if necessary. Reading Law 16.7.1 gives the three-step administration (warning, fault if previously warned, fault for flagrant offence), and Law 16.7.2 gives the Referee's power to disqualify after a fault. ITTO 5.17.3 and 5.17.4 give the umpire's actual calls (yellow card warning, red card fault), and ITTO 5.10.4 covers having the wet court mopped. Together these fully answer the question.
answer.answer: Under Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, clause 5.9.1.6, a player throwing sweat or otherwise contaminating the court and its immediate surroundings 'shall be reminded that such conduct is unacceptable, with Law 16.7 applied, if necessary'. If Law 16.7 is applied, the umpire administers the breach under Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 16.7.1 by: (1) issuing a warning to the offending side (Law 16.7.1.1) — per ITTO 5.17.3 the umpire calls 'Come here' and '… [name of player], warning for misconduct' while raising a yellow card; (2) faulting the offending side if previously warned (Law 16.7.1.2) — per ITTO 5.17.4 the umpire calls '… [name of player], fault for misconduct' with a red card and must call the Referee on court and report immediately; or (3) faulting the offending side in cases of flagrant offence or breach (Law 16.7.1.3). On faulting a side, Law 16.7.2 provides that 'the umpire shall report the offending side immediately to the Referee, who shall have the power to disqualify the offending side from the match'. Separately, if the court becomes wet, ITTO 5.10.4 provides that the players indicate to the Court Attendants where mopping is needed and 'shall be on court as soon as the wiping is over and before the Court Attendants leave the court'.

question: The line judge couldn't see whether the shuttle landed in. What happens to the rally?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what happens to the rally when a line judge could not see whether the shuttle landed in. The directly on-point source is Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) Clause 14.2.6, which makes it a 'let' when a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision. Laws 14.1 and 14.3 explain what a let means for the rally: play since the last service does not count and the last server serves again. The Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) Clauses 8.5 and 8.8 cover the line judge's unsighted signal (hands over eyes; 'UNSIGHTED' hand signal). Together these fully answer the question.
answer.answer: If the line judge is unsighted, it is a 'let' — but only if the umpire or the Instant Review System is unable to make the decision. Under Law 14.2.6 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, it shall be a 'let' if 'a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision'. When a let occurs, Law 14.3 states: 'play since the last service shall not count and the player who served last shall serve again' — so the rally is replayed from the same service with no point scored. The umpire calls 'let' to halt play (Law 14.1). Meanwhile, the line judge should immediately signal that they were unsighted: per Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), Clause 8.5, 'If unsighted, inform the Umpire immediately by putting both hands up to cover the eyes', and 'UNSIGHTED' is one of the approved hand signals (Clause 8.8).

question: Can my coach get up from his chair and stand at the side of the court during the match?

answer.reasoning: The question asks whether a coach may stand at the side of the court during a match. The Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), Clause 5.12.2 directly answers this: coaches must be seated in designated seats and must not stand court-side during the match except during the permitted intervals in Law 16.2. Clause 5.12.1 adds that coaching is not allowed once players take up position to serve and while the shuttle is in play. Law 16.2 (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2)) defines those permitted intervals: not exceeding 60 seconds during each game when the leading score reaches 11 (16.2.1), and not exceeding 120 seconds between games (16.2.2). Together these sources fully answer the question, so no refusal is needed.
answer.answer: No. Under the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.12.2 (Coaching from Off Court), "Coaches must be seated in their designated seats and must not stand court-side during the match except during the permitted intervals (Law 16.2)." The only exceptions are the intervals allowed by Law 16.2 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26: an interval "not exceeding 60 seconds during each game when the leading score reaches 11 points, except Handicap matches" (Law 16.2.1) and an interval "not exceeding 120 seconds between the first and second game, and between the second and third game" (Law 16.2.2). In addition, Clause 5.12.1 states that "Coaching is not allowed from the moment the players have taken up position to serve and receive the next service, and while the shuttle is in play," so even between rallies the coach coaches from the seat, not by standing at the court. If a coach disrupts play or distracts an opponent by standing, Law 14.2.5 provides it shall be a 'let' "if: in the opinion of the umpire, play is disrupted or a player of the opposing side is distracted by a coach."

question: What weight range is allowed for a plastic shuttle, and since our hall gets really hot and stuffy in summer, can we use a special type made for hot weather?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) the allowed weight of a plastic (non-feathered/synthetic) shuttle, and (2) whether a special hot-weather shuttle type may be used. Laws 2.3.3 and 2.2.6 answer the weight part: a non-feathered shuttle must meet the feathered shuttle's weight of 4.74–5.50 grams, with up to 10 per cent variation acceptable for synthetic materials. Law 2.4 answers the hot-weather part: the Laws recognize no special 'hot weather' shuttle; modifications to the specifications are allowed only with the approval of the Member Association concerned, only where atmospheric conditions due to altitude or climate make the standard shuttle unsuitable, and only subject to no variation in general design, speed and flight. ITTO 3.5.4.7 adds that shuttles should be retested if temperature/humidity change substantially, which is about testing existing shuttles, not a special type. Together the sources answer both parts.
answer.answer: Weight: A plastic (non-feathered) shuttle's measurements and weight must be as for a feathered shuttle — Law 2.2.6 sets the shuttle weight at 4.74 to 5.50 grams — but because synthetic materials differ in specific gravity from feathers, Law 2.3.3 allows a variation of up to 10 per cent (i.e. roughly 4.27 to 6.05 grams). Hot weather: The Laws do not provide a special 'hot weather' shuttle type. Under Law 2.4, modifications to the shuttle specifications may be made only with the approval of the Member Association concerned, and only in places where atmospheric conditions due to altitude or climate make the standard shuttle unsuitable — and even then subject to there being no variation in the general design, speed and flight of the shuttle. Separately, the Instructions to Technical Officials say shuttles should be retested if playing conditions such as temperature and humidity change substantially, but that concerns testing standard shuttles, not using a different type. So in your hot hall you should use a compliant shuttle of the correct speed (the Referee is the sole judge of shuttle speed), and any modified shuttle would need your Member Association's approval under Law 2.4.

question: My opponent got a yellow card for swearing during the warm-up, before the umpire called 'Play'. Does it cost him a point now, and does the card go on his record after the tournament?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) whether a yellow card for misconduct before 'Play' costs a point, and (2) whether the card stays on the player's record after the tournament. itto-5.17.10 directly answers part 1: misconduct before 'Play' is carded as usual, but 'Any card(s) given shall have no effect on the score of the match', while still counting if further offences occur during the match (Law 16.7.1.2, which says the umpire faults a side 'if previously warned'). Part 2 is covered by itto-5.17.2 (umpire must 'Record and report to the Referee any incident of misconduct and the action taken') and itto-3.7.3 (after the tournament the Referee sends BWF/CC 'a report on withdrawals, yellow and red cards, that may trigger further sanctions'). The sources do not say anything about cards being expunged or a permanent record beyond this reporting, so I state exactly what they cover. The swearing itself falls under Law 16.6.3 ('behave in an offensive or inappropriate manner'), and the yellow card procedure is itto-5.17.3 / Law 16.7.1.1.
answer.answer:
No, it does not cost him a point. Under Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) (in force 2025-04-26), Clause 5.17.10: 'Misconduct before the match while on the Field Of Play before "Play" has been called at the start of the match, shall be treated as in Instructions 5.17.3, 5.17.4 or 5.17.5. Any card(s) given shall have no effect on the score of the match but a card(s) shall be taken into account if further offences occur during the match (Law 16.7.1.2).' So the yellow card is administered normally (swearing is 'behave in an offensive or inappropriate manner' under Law 16.6.3 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, warned under Law 16.7.1.1 with a yellow card per ITTO 5.17.3), but it has no effect on the score. However, because Law 16.7.1.2 says the umpire faults the offending side 'if previously warned', the pre-match card counts: if he commits a further offence during the match, he is faulted, which costs the point at that time.

Yes, the card goes on record and is reported beyond the match. The Umpire must 'Record and report to the Referee any incident of misconduct and the action taken' (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 5.17.2), and 'The Referee shall immediately after the tournament send to BWF (or CC) a report on withdrawals, yellow and red cards, that may trigger further sanctions' (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 3.7.3). The sources do not state any rule expunging the card or limiting how long it remains on record; what they cover is that the card is recorded, reported to the Referee, and included in the post-tournament report to BWF (or CC) that may trigger further sanctions.
